title: The world is heating up catastrophically yet climate action is in chaos. What happened? | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

Fossil fuels have been on a winning streak this month — even if some global leaders wouldrather not mention them at all.

At the first ever US-China-Russia leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen, China, last week, President Donald Trump, China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin put out ajoint statementpledging to ramp up oil production and supply.

Around 5,000 miles to the west, in the Mediterranean tourist city of Antalya, Turkey, the COP31climate summit broke downover whether moving away from fossil fuels — the very drivers of the climate crisis — would be mentioned at all in a final deal, intended to set priorities for tackling the global crisis.

Catastrophicfloods,fires,heat wavesand more powerfulstormshave swept the planet this year, underscoring the visceral horrors of climate change.

Yet, climate action on the global policy stage appears to be weakening and fossil fuels keep on winning. So, how did we get here?

Three years ago, the world looked to be in a different place. Countries at COP28 in Dubai agreed to an unprecedentedcall to transition away from fossil fuels, the first time these two words had appeared in a COP climate deal.

It seemed to signal a real shift. But petrostates such as Saudi Arabia and Russia have since demonstrated “buyer’s remorse,” said Alden Meyer, a senior associate of the climate change think tank E3G. They have fought against any subsequent inclusion of the words “fossil fuels” — and have been remarkably successful.

What happened in Turkey “is clearly an effort by a handful of energy-exporting states to block action that will reduce demand for their product and their profits,” Meyer said.

Some oil-producing countries pushed instead for commitments to aggressively ramp up carbon capture, a technology that sucks up climate pollution from fossil fuel facilities but which is unproven at scale, expensive and currently used mostly to squeeze more oil and gas from aging fields.

Petrostates have been aided by geopolitical headwinds. Global attention is diverted by conflicts — including the Iran war. And in the United States, the Trump administration has called climate change “nonsense,” is laser-focused on boosting fossil fuels and has pulled the country out of international climate action, meaning the US is now a COP no-show.

While the US was often accused of lacking ambition at climate talks, its negotiators were also known for their ability to gently coax petrostates into more ambitious collective action.

But it’s not just the petrostates that “stand exposed” when it comes to a lack of ambition, said Harjeet Singh, a COP negotiations veteran and founding director of Satat Sampada Climate Foundation. Many of the countries that portray themselves as climate leaders internationally are busy approving oil and gas projects at home.

The United Kingdom has just approved thedevelopment of Jackdaw, a major new gas field in the North Sea, and is debating approving a huge North Sea oil field; Canada is backing a new pipeline to carrya million barrels of oil a day to Asia; and Ireland — whose climate minister called a COP31 deal silent on fossil fuels “unconscionable” — is pushing ahead with a new import terminal for liquified natural gas.

There are silver linings in the failed COP31 deal, experts say. “Petrostates and rich polluters failed to get countries to endorse a text that would have moved the world backward on climate action,” said Mohamed Adow, founding director of the think tank Power Shift Africa.

The drama of COP31’s breakdown may ultimately backfire on oil-producing nations by generating more of a sense of crisis and by helping to forge closer relationships between countries pushing for more ambition, Meyer said.

He also stressed that COP31 was not a total bust. The overarching deal was rejected but other actions were agreed on. Around80 countriespledged to boost the electrification of their economies and more than 30 countries aredeveloping roadmapsto move away from fossil fuels.

There’s also the real-world action, outside the COP conference halls. Wind and solar energy costs are plummeting and clean energy isgrowing at record pace.

War and conflicts have revealed the perils of a global fossil fuel-powered energy system thatrelies heavily on a few chokepoints in volatile regions.

Iran’s restrictions on the Strait of Hormuz, a key oil and gas transport route, sent energy prices soaring and contributed to a wave of cost-of-living pressures.

Renewable energy is increasingly seen as a path to energy security for oil and gas-importing nations as they’re able harness the wind and sun on their own land.

“Petrostates are fighting so hard precisely because the economics have turned against them,” Singh said. “But they’re winning on the politics, and that’s why we’re going backwards.”
